demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
keep mind occupied all the time
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.explanation: The threat items are centered on assault/home-intrusion danger (noticing weapons, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of unexpected death of a loved one. Hypervigilance alone could fit PTSD broadly, but these two specific items imply a different trauma context.

Drop Responsibilities is framed as giving up responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers. In this profile, the listed triggers node is absent and the rest of the profile is dominated by grief/loss-linked appraisals and memory disturbance rather than a coherent pattern of situational avoidance for physical safety. That makes this specific strategy item poorly matched to the other selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring implies an ongoing interpersonal/home-invasion danger context. For trauma type of unexpected death of a loved one, this is hard to reconcile unless additional assault-related trauma is present. It also sits poorly with the formulation because Triggers→Threat is inactive, yet the threat content is highly specific to external intrusion rather than generalized post-loss threat.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is more consistent with trauma involving personal failure, assault, or injury than bereavement-focused PTSD. After unexpected death of a loved one, appraisals would more plausibly center on guilt, loss, permanent change, or the world being unsafe. 'I am a weak person' and 'I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me' are not impossible, but together they pull toward a different trauma formulation and are weakly anchored to the rest of the profile.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, the memory profile is largely grief/intrusion based, but 'Rage on Recall' stands out as difficult to reconcile with the rest of this profile because no other items indicate anger-focused appraisals, perpetrator blame, or threat-related meaning that would explain intense rage as the dominant recall response.

The Threat items describe a sustained current-danger state ('superalert', 'constantly tense and ready to react to danger'), but the formulation contains no active links into Threat and the other selected nodes are centered on loss, permanent change, numbing, and intrusive fragmented memory. This level of ongoing danger-readiness is not well integrated with the rest of the profile and appears clinically disconnected rather than supported by the appraisals or memory content.

vignette:
Amina is a 33-year-old married woman who had worked for years as a park ranger, a role that once gave shape to how she saw herself: capable, watchful, physically competent, and at ease outdoors. She came to treatment after the unexpected death of her younger brother, who had been visiting from out of state and joined her for a day in the park where she worked. He died there in an accident so abrupt that Amina still speaks of it as if time split open around a handful of images. She remembers the day in sharp visual stills rather than as a flowing sequence: the angle of his body near a rocky drop-off, the color of his jacket against the dirt, his face for one impossible second before she reached him. Those images arrive without warning and vanish just as quickly, leaving her shaken and full of grief. When they come, she does not describe “thinking about” what happened so much as seeing photographs in her mind that she never chose to look at.

In the first weeks after his death, Amina returned home to her husband carrying a kind of stunned horror that sat alongside raw grief. She found that whenever the memory surfaced, the grief was immediate and overwhelming, as if the loss were happening again in that instant. At other times she felt frighteningly cut off from herself, telling her husband she felt dead inside and unlike the woman she had been before. She had come to believe that something in her had been permanently damaged. The work that used to define her now seemed to belong to someone else. Before, she had taken pride in being the ranger people relied on in difficult conditions; now she was certain she was no longer capable of being that person.

As the months passed, her days became organized around getting through without being caught off guard. At work, the trails, lookout points, emergency radio calls, and even casual talk with visitors about scenic overlooks could turn into specific moments of danger for her, because they brought her back to the place where her brother died. Rather than taking on the duties she once handled confidently, she started giving up important responsibilities. She asked coworkers to cover trail patrols that involved steep areas and avoided assignments that might bring her near the site. The changes were noticeable. Tasks she would once have volunteered for were quietly passed on, and she felt ashamed watching others absorb parts of the job she believed used to prove who she was.

Outside work, Amina kept her mind occupied almost constantly. If she was home, the television was on, or she scrolled on her phone while doing chores, or found something practical to clean, sort, or organize. Silence felt risky. Relaxation felt worse. She stopped sitting quietly on the porch with her husband in the evenings, something they had once enjoyed, because stillness made her feel exposed, as though letting her guard down would allow the images in. She did not trust calm; she experienced it as dangerous. Her body rarely softened. She described herself as always braced, shoulders tight, hearing small noises and reacting before she had time to think. At night she struggled to fall asleep, and when she did sleep it was light and easily broken. Bedtime itself had become difficult because there was less to distract her there.

Her husband had tried to reach her in her grief, but he increasingly met either intensity or distance. There were times she was flooded with fear, anger, guilt, and sorrow; other times she seemed emotionally absent, unable to connect even when she wanted to. What frightened her most was not only that she had lost her brother, but that she had changed into someone diminished and permanently estranged from the life that once fit her. Being a park ranger had been central to her sense of self, and each accommodation at work felt like evidence that this version of her was gone.

She finally sought help after a recent shift in which a family asked her for directions to a viewpoint, and the request instantly brought up one of those visual fragments of the day her brother died. For a few seconds she could only see the scene in flashes, and afterward she was overcome by grief so strong she had to step away and ask a colleague to take over. Driving home, tense and exhausted after another night of poor sleep, she realized how much of her life had narrowed. She came in hoping, cautiously, that she might find some way to live without feeling either ambushed by those images or emptied out by them. At the same time, she was afraid that treatment would confirm what she already believed: that the capable woman she had been is gone for good.
